At a value of less than 80 per cent of the American dollar, the low Canadian dollar should be drawing record numbers of American tourists to our beautiful country but, instead, travel to Canada by Americans this summer has dropped badly, up to 30 per cent in some areas. That this House demands that the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism do everything in his power to let Americans know what a bargain it is to holiday in Canada.

subsubtopic: HONDURAS-INVOLVEMENT WITH NEIGHBOURING COUNTRIES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on the urgent matter of deterioration of peace and international order. Present deliberations by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on Canada's relations with Latin America and the Caribbean are testimony to the fact that this House, and Canadians, are critically concerned about events in that part of the world. Honduran armed forces and mercenary involvement in two neighbouring countries, El Salvador and Nicaragua, has now been made clear. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller):
That this House and the Canadian government protest growing military assistance by Honduras to El Salvador, continuing Honduran armed forces harassment of border area refugees, and Honduran based mercenary attacks on Nicaragua; and that Canada review the status of Honduras as our targeted country in Central America for foreign aid.

FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AFFAIRS DUPLICATION OF SERVICES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, bearing in mind the desire of most Canadians to have the federal government reduce its deficit, now accumulated to a total of $135 billion, a deficit which is known to create an unacceptably high level of taxation, both direct and indirect, as demonstrated by the fact that when Canadians purchase $15 worth of gasoline they pay only $5 for gas and a whopping $10 in taxes, and in light of the study commissioned by the western provincial governments which identified 100 areas where duplication

July 16, 1982
exists in federal and provincial services, and the western premiers' task force on constitutional trends third report, which identifies nine areas of duplication which should receive immediate action for efficiency, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That this House recommends that an all-party parliamentary committee be struck to consider the suggestions of the western premiers with respect to duplication of services by government and that that committee report to Parliament in the fall of 1982 with the objective of pointing out where the Government of Canada, via co-operation, can save taxpayers' dollars.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. FUNDING OF SCHOOL SUPPLIES FOR STUDENTS LIVING OFF RESERVE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has arbitrarily and unilaterally cut off financial assistance for instructional supplies for elementary and secondary school children of treaty Indians who live off reserve in Alberta. This attack on the treaty rights of indigenous peoples is in direct opposition to the Government of Canada's legal obligation to uphold its treaty commitments. Approximately 20 per cent of Alberta treaty Indians are forced to live off reserve because of the lack of viable economic development activity within the reserves. Whereas the fully sanctioned rights of treaty Indians are not to be denied because of place of residence, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That this directive be immediately withdrawn and that the treaty Indian students of Alberta be assured that the right to education will be respected, and further, that this government recommit itself to meaningful dialogue with the native peoples of Canada, reject unilateral action, and uphold the recently endorsed Charter of Rights.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In the first six months of this year compared to last year farm bankruptcies in Quebec are up 243 per cent, 533 per cent in Manitoba, and over 60 per cent in Canada as a whole. Since farmers are facing a 17 per cent decrease in their net income this year over last-we do not even have the figures for forced farm liquidations-can the minister state that his present economic policies, which may help only 600 of the over 300,000 farmers in Canada, are adequate to meet our food production requirements?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe the hon. member will have to make up his own mind on that subject. In my view the policies put in place in the budget are essential to bring about recovery in the Canadian economy. The way to succeed, the way to improve the situation, is to make the

July 16, 1982
Oral Questions
difficult changeover from the 12 per cent society we are presently in to a 6 per cent society. That is the basic approach of the government, and I believe it will lead to success. 1 hope the hon. member will find that approach satisfying and will join the growing number of Canadians who now see the justification for the approach taken by the government.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: That is little comfort to the hundreds and hundreds of farmers being forced off their farms by high interest rates, taxes, and product prices far below the cost of production.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, bearing in mind that the average age of Canadian farmers is in excess of 50 years, and noting that the majority of bankruptcies are the young farmers of this nation who are attempting to put into practice the most advanced technical methods in the field of agriculture, what real assurances can the Minister of Finance give this country that there will be people to take over from the older farmers who are retiring? Why will he not act quickly to bring about some real interest rate relief for this sector, and move in the farm fuel tax area? Can he not give these young farmers some hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member will recall that in the budget there is additional support for farmers facing financial difficulty, and a program will be administered through the Farm Credit Corporation which will substantially reduce the interest costs of farmers. That is a very important step taken in the budget.
The hon. member is quite right in underlining the importance of bringing down interest rates, and I am encouraged by the report yesterday that the bank rate and the prime rate have both decreased, in combination with a strengthening of the Canadian dollar. Both those trends justify the policy course established by the government in the recent budget.

subsubtopic: TAX ON FUEL USED IN FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. On January 31, 1980, during the last election campaign, the Minister of Agriculture, in a speech in Alvinston, Ontario, stated the following:
Fuels used in farm production will be exempt from any excise tax and a special price structure established.
What happened to that price structure? Why has the minister not been able to convince his cabinet colleagues to relieve the farmers of Canada from the federal rip-off of 60 cents a gallon on the price of farm fuel, constituting some 40 per cent of the price? if the minister is not able to convince his cabinet colleagues to fulfil his election promise, why does he not do the honourable thing and resign?

subsubtopic: DOFASCO ANNOUNCEMENT OF FALL LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. We were all shocked at the announcement by Dofasco that 2,100 employees will receive indefinite lay-off notices to be effective in October and November, and that, if there is not a turnaround in the economy, a second wave of lay-offs may be necessary.
Dofasco is one of the most stable employers on this continent, with good productivity levels and high morale. In fact its advertisements state "its strength is people". Inasmuch as the thrust of the budget is restraint, which will have little immediate effect on the market supplied by Dofasco, can the minister advise whether he can see any options open to the government that will hold off the second wave of lay-offs suggested by Dofasco?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: DOFASCO ANNOUNCEMENT OF FALL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member is aware of the budget provisions. What I know about the situation is that these lay-offs are not to take place for some time, that Dofasco has all the good assets which the hon. member has mentioned, and because of that it has been operating close to capacity. It is projecting these lay-offs because of a decline in economic activity and because of the recession. I assure the hon. member that the quickest way to assist Dofasco and other firms is to succeed in reducing inflation in this country and to put ourselves on the road to recovery by reducing the rate of inflation from close to 12 per cent to 6 per cent. I enlist the hon. member's support in that campaign in the months ahead.

The minister knows that Dofasco feeds the automotive industry, the heavy transportation industry, and the appliance and housing industries. The appliance industry is tied directly to housing starts. The automobile industry is not operating at anywhere near capacity, and the downturn in heavy transportation can be linked directly to the national energy policy.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 also want to ask the Minister of Finance a question related in many ways to the questions just asked. He will be aware that in the announcement by Dofasco it indicated that it was not its overseas or out-of-the-country sales that were the problem primarily, that it was its domestic sales which had dropped off so dramatically that the company was now faced with, or at least was announcing the lay-off of almost 20 per cent of its work force.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and it is supplementary to that put to her by the hon. member for Niagara Falls. As the minister knows, there is a division of opinion in the medical profession on the use of heroin and its effectiveness as a pain killer for patients who are terminally ill, the victims of cancer or other dreadful diseases. There is also a division in the House, I am sure, but from information which I am prepared to give to the minister there seems to be considerable support among the general public for the proposition that it be used as a pain killer, especially in the treatment of these patients.

Given this division of opinion, even in the medical profession, would the minister consider permitting the appropriate standing committee of this House, as one possible instrument, to look at the proposition so that the debate on the matter could be opened to the public and so that those organizations and groups, including the medical profession, which have some views on the matter, could deal with the question? speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is asking me for a step to bring the miners back to work. I hope he understands that the situation is a little more complicated than one that can be solved by taking a single step. The mineral industry is in trouble, because of a recession that is
July 16, 1982

world-wide and a recession that is being experienced very deeply in this country. speechtext: With reference to the estimates of the Department of the Solicitor General at p. 27.13, volume II of the 1980-81 Public Accounts of Canada (a) how does the Solicitor General explain the increase in revenue for the RCMP from "Proceeds in Sales" from zero in the fiscal year 1979-80 to $3,494,568 in 1980-81 (b) what is the explanation for the increase from zero to $13,532 under the heading "Proceeds from the sale of ammunition to members"?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: RCMP- PUBLIC ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
1. (a) Up to and
including 1979-80, the RCMP was authorized to use working capital advances for clothing and kit procurement/distribution (sale of uniform cloth to manufacturers, purchase back of finished garments from manufacturers, sale of kit to members and to provincial auxiliary units) and mess operations (purchase of raw food, cash sales and payroll deductions on meals provided to personnel). The revenues shown after the first five items under the "Proceeds from Sales" heading in 1980-81 public accounts were credited against expenditures within the above working capital advances in 1979-80 and, therefore, would not be considered as non-tax revenue for reporting purposes.
The above working capital advances were ordered cancelled by the Treasury Board effective 1980-81. Expenditures previously charged to these advances became chargeable to the RCMP Vote 15 and revenues previously credited there were deposited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This explains the appearance of the first five items under the "Proceeds from Sales" for the first time in 1980-81 public accounts.
The remaining two minor items under the heading "Proceeds from Sales" in the 1980-81 Public Accounts were "vote netted" up to and including 1979-80 and therefore not shown as non-tax revenue. In order to more accurately reflect RCMP operations and improve visibility within financial statements, these items were recorded as revenue credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund commencing 1980-81.
(b) Comparable sales of ammunition to members of the force, for purposes of weaponry proficiency, were made in 1979-80 but "vote netted" as opposed to being credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. These sales were credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund in 1980-81. See also the answer to part (a) above.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the House adjourned last night I had listed three alternatives, or three policy decisions that the government could make. 1 am struck by what I can only call the sleazy discussion of the Conservative Party, a recent example of which is the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) which were typical of their McCarthyite paranoia.
Bill C-124 has been called unfair by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), it has been called unfair by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) and it has been called unfair by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). All three hon. members say they will vote for unfairness, Mr. Speaker. They are all in favour of unfairness.
This coalition of Conservatives and Liberals, this coalition of the right, of the reactionaries who have not learned anything since the dirty thirties, means that the first victims of inflation are being attacked-the low-income earners and old age pensioners. These great official opposition Conservatives support the Liberal government in chiselling old people out of a few dollars a year. It is plain chiselling and I have to use the word sleazy.
As an innocent prairie boy I still want to learn something and I need some more instruction and explanation from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on how higher interest rates mean lower inflation. I still cannot figure that out. In this country higher interest rates have meant higher inflation. That has resulted in people losing their homes, people losing jobs, people losing farms and people losing businesses. But somehow or other, as R. B. Bennett and Mackenzie King proclaimed in '32, '34 and '37, keeping interest rates high was supposed to solve our problems.
Last night I suggested that the Government of Canada should declare a state of national economic emergency and do what was done when there was a declaration of war, only this time it should be a declaration of peace with all that that implies. It should be a declaration of peace that puts people in Canada to work, because there is so much to do.
The Conservatives want to vote for Liberals unfairness, Mr. Speaker, but may I suggest an alternative. For those who earn more than $75,000 or $100,000 per year-pick your own figure-we should amend the Income Tax Act and tax the amount of increases back 100 per cent. Anyone earning less

July 16, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
than $20,000 or $25,000 per year-pick your figure, maybe $30,000-should be left alone. They are not the cause of inflation, they are the victims-the first victims of it. Surely if the government were to blow the dust off the report of the Carter Royal Commission of 1966 and bring in revised income tax provisions and tax people on the ability to pay, then, if you were fighting inflation, you would first of all tax those who cause inflation. They are the profit takers and money takers- not the profit makers but profit takers. An income tax act should allow a reasonable return of profit, a reasonable return on investment. Anything beyond that should be regarded as pure selfishness and greed. The money changers have snuck in the back door of the temple again and the Grits and Tories keep them there.
As I said yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the first target is interest rates. Until they are brought down nothing else will decrease. The costs of that policy are greater than the costs of inflation. The cost of high interest rates has caused the lay-offs in our steel industry at Ipsco, Dofasco and others and also in the forest industry. The evidence is in, Mr. Speaker; high interest rates mean higher and continued high inflation.
In 117 years we have had Conservative governments, Liberal governments, Conservative governments, Liberal governments, Liberal governments, Conservative governments and Liberal governments. For all the barbs that are thrown around, Mr. Speaker, I do not know of any social democrats or democratic socialists who have brought these policies about. Why blame me? I am NDP.
It was not the wild-eyed radicals, the wild-eyed socialists, who put 1,300,000 people out of work in this country. It was not wild-eyed socialists who caused the bankruptcies of hundreds of farmers and thousands of small-business men. It was the free enterprise Grits and Tories and their alliance that preserved a system that has outlived its usefulness. They do not have the courage and imagination to make fundamental changes in the direction, the nature and the purpose of our system. The appeal to greed and selfishness, to make all you can and to hell with everybody else, perpetuated by Liberals and Tories for 117 years in this country still continues. That alliance is unethical, unchristian, unseemly and obscene.
I want to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this Parliament should stay here and make a fundamental change in what the government is proposing. It should do that as we did in wartime. We declare a national economic emergency and do as we did then. We challenge Canadians because we have energetic and hardworking people, we have the money and the resources. We should invest-not spend-in the creation of employment and the satisfying of the genuine needs of the Canadian population. That means $1 billion a year for the next five years in housing, the ramifications of which are obvious. It means $1 billion a year for the next 15 years invested in transportation, and the ramifications of that are obvious. It means further large investment in the production of food. We can do it, Mr. Speaker, so for a change let us do what this country is capable of doing. Let us make a declaration of peace, as we did when we made a declaration of war. We have had enough of these frightened and small-minded men who cannot change their minds. We have had enough of the old parties and the old policies.
I have quoted ministers of finance and leaders of the opposition, both Grit and Tory, from 1932 to 1938. We get the same kind of speeches and the same kind of budgets out of the same kind of Liberals and the same kind of Tories now as we did in the dirty thirties. Mr. Speaker, this Parliament should sit and make a declaration of a national economic emergency and turn this country back to work; we are capable of doing it and have the resources to do it with.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-124 respecting compensation in the public sector, and to explain why I strongly support the leadership the government is giving with this bill to resurrect our economy with a new 6 per cent society. I do want to say, though, to my respected friend, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), concerning his comments about the free enterprise system, that it was this system, the working relationship between the public and private sectors and the ingenuity of Canadians, which built this country into the great society we
July 16, 1982

have today. 1 do not think it was some of the policies he has been advocating in his speech, as much as I respect him as a friend, which built Canada into one of the greatest nations in the world.
There have been many speeches in this House, Mr. Speaker, in the past week, on this bill, with I think some very constructive suggestions which my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), has indicated will be listened to in committee by the government before the bill comes back to the House for report stage and third reading. In the debate the details of the cause of inflation, our present economic situation and the OECD report have been outlined by several speakers.
In particular, I would commend hon. members to read the speech of our colleague, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), who I thought gave a very competent speech with respect to the situation and how we can resurrect our domestic situation. I would like to divide my speech into two parts, one with respect to my specific responsibilities concerning trade- because there have been many comments made by hon. members on both sides during the past week about the importance to Canada of exports and how they can lead us out of the present economic situation we are experiencing. Second, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments as an individual Canadian and Member of Parliament.
First of all, in reading some of the speeches I see that there has been a substantial lack of understanding of what the export market means to Canada, its makeup and mix, and how it affects the various regions of this country. Much of the viability of the Canadian economy as a major trading entity depends upon its ability to compete in export markets. This in essence is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is doing in trying to get Canada back to a 6 per cent society and make us more competitive. Almost one third of Canada's GNP is generated by trade in goods and services.
Approximately one-third of all goods manufactured in this country are destined for export markets. It is estimated that almost two million jobs in the manufacturing sector alone are directly the result of the production of goods and services for export. It represents roughly 20 per cent of the total labour market and work force in this country. I think it is imperative that we all understand the significance and magnitude of these facts. Our trade performance has allowed Canadian industry to specialize and become more efficient. It has encouraged investment, both domestic and foreign. Above all, it has brought real income gains and higher living standards to Canadian workers.
Equally imperative is the need for Canada to maintain and improve its international competitiveness. Failure to do so will harm Canadian industry, discourage investment, and erode the living standards of all Canadians. Today inflation is eating away at our competitiveness. It is no accident-and I think this was alluded to by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, in response to a question this morning-that Japan and the Federal Republic of Germany, the two industrialized countries which have been most successful recently in penetrating
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
foreign markets recently, have also enjoyed the lowest rates of inflation within the OECD countries.
Canadian wage and price performance has recently moved seriously out of line with that of our major trading partners. For a country like Canada, with such an open economy, so dependent on trade for its economic wellbeing, it is important that our wage and price structure, as well as other cost components, not move out of phase with those prevailing in our major markets. We simply cannot afford a loss of international competitiveness. Devaluation offers no long-term, viable solution. We must bring inflation under control. We are asking all Canadians to take up this challenge and join with us in our fight against inflation.
I want to spend a few moments talking about Canada's recent trade performance, Mr. Speaker,-the changing composition of Canadian trade, and the reasons why it is so crucial for our future trade success to get better control of our wage-price performance. Recent Canadian trade performance remains a bright spot and source of strength for the Canadian economy. We have had a trade surplus for over 24 consecutive months, a record matched by very few countries in the world. Our over-all surplus in the trade of goods during the last 12 calendar months is approximately $10.4 billion.
During the first five months of this year our merchandise trade balance was running at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of nearly $15 billion. We registered a current account surplus in the first quarter of this year. While the services deficit is increasing, we anticipate the current account will be in near balance for all of 1982. Contrast this with the massive merchandising trade deficit which the United States has incurred during the last couple of years and also the European community. You will see that this indeed is a bright spot in the Canadian economy.
In the 1981 calendar year, Canada achieved its second highest ever merchandise trade surplus of $7.4 billion. This came about as the value of exports increased 10 per cent. The volume of exports in real terms increased by over 3 per cent. These gains occurred in a year when world trade actually fell.
A very significant point which should be understood by all our colleagues here in the House is that while international trade fell, Canada had record trade surpluses during this two-year period. This was achieved in a time of little or no world growth and it enabled Canada to increase its share of world markets to 3.6 per cent from 3.2 percent in the preceding year. More important is that Canada's share of manufactured exports to developed country markets increased to 4.2 per cent from 3.7 per cent. The fact that we are increasing our share of markets when the world market was down augurs well for the future of all Canadians when the world economy turns around.
This marks another important feature that I want to highlight for you, Mr. Speaker. It is the labour-intensive side of our trade, the manufacturing side, not just end products but also

July 16, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
semi-processed goods. The most important gains which Canada achieved in the value of exports in 1981 came from three of the four top segments in the manufacturing sector. This reflects the dramatic increases over the last 20 years of the share of manufactured products in Canada's export trade.
In 1961, finished manufactured goods represented 8.8 per cent of Canadian exports. In 1981, this share stood at 31.2 per cent. In the first five months of this year, this share is showing increased strength. Unfortunately, this is a fact little known and little appreciated by Canadians.
Many Canadians have been concerned about our perceived role as "hewers of wood and drawers of water". Of course, Canada has been blessed with a large resource endowment in agriculture, minerals, forestry and energy. Canadians have built on this strength and we should make no apologies about this fact. It means that Canada does not need to import these products and that Canada has a much wider range of products available for export. But this does not mean that Canada is not a major exporter of manufactured products as well.
There is a mistaken tendency to consider that only end products, as defined by Statistics Canada in its commodity trade classification, can be classified as manufactured goods. According to this definition, only about 30 per cent of Canada's total exports in value terms would have qualified as manufactured exports in 1980. Elowever, if one broadens the definition to Statistics Canada's industrial classification, fabricated materials, primary manufactured, and end products, finished manufactured, as well as certain processed food products, we would find that over 70 per cent of Canada's total exports on a value basis would have qualified as "manufactured goods" exports.
For the purpose of making some international comparisons let us use the official United Nations definition for manufactured goods. On the basis of this definition, 55.4 per cent of Canada's total value of exports was classified as manufactured goods exports in 1979. This is in the same range as that of Denmark, The Netherlands and Norway and considerably ahead of Australia's 23.4 per cent. The U.S., which is considered to be the industrial giant of the world, has a comparatively moderate 67.4 per cent proportion of its total exports in the manufactured category.
Looking at volume, Canada's manufactured goods exports increased by 52 per cent in the period 1975 to 1981, a faster rate of growth than that achieved by any other industrialized country except Japan. It was considerably faster than the 26 per cent increase for the United States and compares favourably with the 37 per cent increase for the total European Community.
Another major element in our strong trade performance has been our success in winning major capital projects with the support of the Export Development Corporation. Capital projects have been a major priority for this government during the last couple of years for three simple reasons. First, success in projects means sales of capita! goods, which is the labourintensive side of trade. Capital goods sales will accrue to all regions in the country if we are successful in capital projects. Second is our image abroad as suppliers of high technology
goods and services, which is increasing dramatically. Third are the success stories which are being passed from one Canadian company to another, thus encouraging more effort in this area.
Never has there been another time in our history when Canadian businessmen and women have been competing for major capital projects around the world in the megaproject range, which we classify as over $100 million. Not only have we been bidding on them but we have been winning these contracts. The best example, I think, is the contract which Bombardier Corporation achieved in New York the other day. It is our largest contract in history, a $1 billion manufacturing contract which really says something for the future of this country.
I think the record speaks for itself. Canada has made significant strides in diversifying its export base and increasing the range of manufactured goods which it exports in addition to its primary goods exports.
A major impetus in our desire to be competitive and in our preparedness to be competitive to this development was the depreciation of the Canadian dollar during the latter half of the 1970s and the fact that wage and price developments were in line or below those of our major trading competitors. This allowed Canadian businessmen to strengthen their role in the world markets and penetrate new ones. However, we cannot always rely on the exchange rate to improve our competitive position. Instead we must achieve this through improving productivity and keeping costs under control.
For example, Canada at mid-1981 ranked sixth among the ten major industrial countries in terms of hourly wage compensation levels in manufacturing. This relative ranking, which has remained reasonably unchanged since the mid-1970s, played a major role in improving Canadian competitiveness. However, the gap in the absolute wage differentials has narrowed considerably since earlier in the 1970s, leaving Sweden as the only country where wage compensation levels were still as much as one fifth higher than in Canada. While we still hold a competitive edge in wage compensation levels in manufacturing, this edge has narrowed considerably since 1980. Small shifts can have a significant impact on our competitiveness.
We have seen the results of what can happen before. In the early 1970s Canadian wage compensation levels were second only to those in the United States. Canadian competitiveness suffered primarily from a decline in productivity and an increase in unit relative to our major trading partners. This led to a swing from a fairly strong surplus to a deficit in merchandise trade and an even greater deficit in the current account. Investment faltered, imports increased and the Canadian manufacturing base suffered.
As I indicated, exchange rate changes and better price-wage performance changed this picture dramatically in the latter part of the 1970s. However, the current level of inflation and increases in unit costs once again threaten our competitive position internationally. In the last quarter of 1981 wage settlements were in the range of 12.7 per cent on average. This compares with a figure of 5.6 per cent in the United States.
July 16, 1982

The U.S. is our largest trading partner representing approximately 65 per cent of our imports and exports. The consequences of such a divergence in our wage, and hence cost, performance, it seems to me, are clear.
Canadian future economic prosperity will be largely influenced by our success in the international marketplace. Yet as we all know, more and more countries are becoming keen exporters as rates of domestic growth slow. As well, recent years have witnessed the emergence of the so-called newly industrializing countries as strong competitors for a broad range of goods. The competition is becoming fierce.
To be successful, Canadian goods will need to be competitive in price, quality and delivery. But there is also another element to success in the international marketplace and that is the role of export financing. Competition in this area, particularly with government supported credits, has become particularly severe. While we have sought to make competitive financing available to Canadian exporters, it is clear that over the longer term Canada cannot hope to win a subsidy battle of national treasuries. The only way to win over the longer term is to lower inflation so as to bring interest rates down and thereby be more competitive in the financing we can offer.
What are the consequences if we fail to act? The most immediate consequence is likely to be a lower merchandise trade surplus. Canada requires a large merchandise trade surplus to balance its current services deficit. In these circumstances a declining surplus can lead only to a higher current account deficit. This, in turn, will impact on the exchange rate. The end result will most likely be even greater inflation and we will be trapped in a vicious circle from which it becomes increasingly difficult to extract ourselves.
Now I should like to turn to the area of domestic effects on trade. I have talked about the role exports play in strengthening Canadian economic performance. But trade plays another role as well in helping to keep inflationary costs down in Canada, and that is through imports. We must not forget that trade is a two-way street. A country can pay for its imports over the longer term only if it earns sufficient foreign exchange through its own exports. Canadian imports help in providing foreigners the means by which to buy our goods. As well, imports provide a source of competition, competition which helps to ensure that we keep our wage and price structure competitive, competition which allows Canadian industry to specialize in the areas where they are most efficient.
In the face of the current recession, we increasingly hear loud voices both in Canada and abroad calling for increased protection against import competition. However, we must avoid resorting to protectionism because of the cyclical downturn. This would not solve the problem of Canadian industry. Protectionism here will only be met by protectionism abroad, and our exports would suffer. Protectionism in Canada would also remove an important stimulant to Canadian industry to adjust and to become more internationally competitive.

There have been exceptional circumstances where the government, as well as our trading partners, have acted to restrict import competition faced by certain industries because of exceptional and special social and economic circumstances. However, I want to reiterate that these are exceptional cases.
These measures are not permanent solutions, and Canadian industry should not consider them as such. The only long-term answer is adjustment and improved competitiveness. Canadian industry must make use of the temporary respite provided to ensure that they are in a position to compete both in Canada and abroad when these special measures are lifted.

As far as our trade interests are concerned, my message to you is very straightforward. The viability of the Canadian economy as a large trading unit depends mostly on Canada's ability to compete on our export markets. This country has made significant strides in diversifying its export base and increasing the range of manufactured goods which it exports abroad. However, prices and wages in Canada are rising dramatically above those of our principal trading partners, especially the United States. The result will be, if we do not act, a decline in our competitiveness internationally and also a decline in our foreign trade balance. This, in turn, would only feed inflation and further complicate an already difficult situation. The only viable solution in the long term is to control inflation and thus improve our cost price.
That is my message. It is a challenge addressed to all Canadians, asking them to help us overcome this crisis.

In my 11 years of public life, Mr. Speaker, this will be the third time that I have participated in a reduction in salary. I think it is important not to use the scapegoat theory. For many of us who come from various professions, we took a substantial cut in compensation to become Members of Parliament, mayors, councillors or provincial legislators. We did not choose this profession because of any monetary gains. For most of us this reduction is what occurred when we first entered public life.
At one time I was the mayor of a community which had the highest unemployment rate in Canada. That was the reason I entered public life. To set an example, I cut my public pay cheque by approximately 10 per cent. I can recall the first negotiation meeting I had when the person opposite me at the table said, "Just because you are foolish does not mean that we have to be." I do not happen to believe in the scapegoat theory, but I believe that these are extraordinary times and, therefore, we must take extraordinary measures.
As I travel across Canada, as I am sure my colleagues on both sides of the House have done, I know the feeling out there is that we in Ottawa are insulated and insensitive to the specific problems faced by Canadians in all walks of life. I am sure my colleagues would agree that in politics perception very quickly becomes reality. It is important that we as parliamentarians, with the control which we have over a substantial portion of the Canadian economy including that with respect

to public servants, should show the leadership necessary to get us out of these economic doldrums.
I happen to be very fortunate to have many dedicated public servants living in my riding. I am not one who thinks that public servants are overpaid and underworked. Collectively, I do not think they are any more overpaid or underworked than people in the private sector. Elaving come from the private sector and having been relatively successful in it, 1 think there are as many mistakes made in the private sector as there are in the public sector. They just do not happen to have all the cameras and media people from across the country watching them as we do in the public sector.
In general, I have found that the public servants with whom I have worked in five different departments since coming to Ottawa are as dedicated as any of the employees I met during my days in the private sector. I think, from talking to rank and file public servants in my constituency and here in Ottawa, they are prepared to accept that leadership role.
I should like to talk about a matter which has affected me personally in the last couple of days. Many hon. members throughout the debate on inflation and unemployment during the past couple of months have talked about the tragedies of individuals who have come to their offices. Two days ago my next door neighbour, my best friend and the father of four children of whom I am the godfather, was killed in a tragic accident. It made the front page of the local newspaper because he was a very dedicated community leader. I want to recite, for the benefit of my colleagues in the House, what happened to this particular gentleman and a partial cause of this sad occasion. I am not attributing any particular blame.
He came to this country over 20 years ago and started at the bottom echelon with a small company employing about 25 people. He worked his way to the top of the company, and at one point where several years ago the company employed 500 people. Then a series of disruptions in the postal service over a period of time totally destroyed his mail order business, so much so that in the last four or five months his company was employing only 25 to 30 people as it had over 20 years ago. For months this gentleman had been fighting to try to save the company, not only for him but for the very dedicated people who worked for him during this 20-year period. He ran back and forth between Cornwall and Montreal, and Ottawa and Toronto trying to find some solution to salvage the company. In this process he wore himself down to the point where he fell asleep driving his car, with the resulting tragic consequences.
There is much human suffering with which we as Members of Parliament are very familiar. When we go to our riding offices on the weekends these people come in to see us. This is why I feel so strongly about this particular bill. No one likes to have something which has been, or is expected to be held back. Those of us who are parents and husbands know that when we have to reduce spending in our own families difficulties occur. Some of us know this as managers in our private lives before becoming parliamentarians.
If we listen to our constituents, as I do, we find that Canadians are thinking more about the future for their children than ever before. One of their great concerns is the legacy which we as a society will leave our children. Will we leave as a society the legacy which our ancestors left us? As parliamentarians and as legislators, I think we grossly underestimate the intelligence of Canadians, their understanding of the problems and their resolve to solve them. Also we underestimate the willingness of Canadians to share the bad times as we shared the good times.
I think the budget of the Minister of Finance helps us to share with those in the system who unfortunately have lost their jobs. If we, not just as the government and public servants, but at every level of government and in every business, commit ourselves to following the leadership set down in this bill, then after a short period of time we would be back on the road to recovery which each and every one of us desires.
Inflation affects everyone. Our legacy is very important. It is not only an individual responsibility, but also it is a collective one. We are asking all Canadians to join us in this challenge. The people of Canada expect leadership to start in Parliament. I sincerely hope that every member in this chamber, regardless of his or her party affiliation, will support this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to put a few comments on the record regarding Bill C-124 as they relate to the Canadian economy as I see it at this time. The first point that I want to make is that I believe restraint in the public sector and the federal government is necessary. It is necessary for a number of reasons. It is necessary when one takes a look at the ever-increasing expenditures that federal governments have been facing and making over the last years. When one takes a further look at the figures, one finds that for every dollar of taxation collected by the federal government-we must keep in mind that these are dollars earned by ordinary Canadians which they have paid in federal taxes- everyone of those after tax dollars uses 23 cents to service the national debt. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the adjournment for lunch I had pointed out that I believe restraint is necessary, but that restraint can only work if the government has a certain amount of credibility, and 1 raised doubts as to that credibility. Specifically in relation to Bill C-124, there have been criticisms that it is not fair. 1 am one who shares that view even though 1 have said that I support a restraint program.
When the bill goes to committee after the vote at four o'clock this afternoon, there are two specific areas that members of that committee should consider; that is, whether Bill C-124 needs to go so far or whether we need to go so far in relation to the terms of collective bargaining. As one reads the bill, one finds that it would put a cap of 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the year thereafter on federal public service salaries. What it also does for that period of time, at least in the practical sense, is that it virtually eliminates collective bargaining.
There are areas in collective bargaining that could be and should be maintained even during that period. 1 will get to those areas, but before doing so I would like to give the reasons why 1 believe that to be the case. I believe that collective bargaining has worked in the public service. If one takes a look at the number of contracts that have been negotiated between the government and the public service, one finds that the number of times where breakdowns occurred is very limited. Granted, some of those were high profile ones. I would like to see some change there concerning essential services, but I am not speaking of essential services at this stage. Members could very quickly say that that refers to the post office, and I agree with them. I think Canadians should be and are entitled to the maintenance of certain services, and Canada Post is an essential service. But by and large, the record of negotiation and agreement around the table between the public service and the federal government has been good.
Should we, through Bill C-124, suspend that process for two years, I question what would be the climate when those two years end in terms of the collective bargaining process between the public service and the federal government. I said I would raise two points which I would think could still remain open for bargaining during that period of time. Other members will, 1 am sure, have other instances to mention. One is the matter of health and safety in the workplace. I have no doubt that the issue of health and safety in the workplace remains a legitimate and valid area of negotiation, even during this two-and-a-half-year period that is to start now. I have federal civil servants in my riding who work, for example, as inspectors in abattoirs. There is often a question of health and safety there that it is necessary to examine and this has to be negotiated.
There is also the question of Revenue Canada employees at the international border. I have a number of ports along the Canadian-United States international border. In fact, a study was done some time ago looking at the danger these men and women are often faced with in their work. For instance, there is the new sophistication of smuggling in the area of drugs. For some period of time they have been working with the department and with the public service trying to develop a plan whereby they could address these new, modern problems that these employees face at the border. I see no reason why in this two-year period that kind of negotiation should not go on. In fact, it should be encouraged to go on.
I also see no difficulty, Mr. Speaker, in continuing the concept of equal pay for work of equal value. Those areas should be continued in negotiation form during the next two years. I do not see how that would affect the restraint program in any way. There might be the argument that there would be some reclassification and therefore there might be some additional cost to the treasury, but I think on balance, for the net return and for the climate we can create, those are two areas to be discussed. I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) that he look at that point seriously in terms of amendments, either from our side or from the government side. We could bring in amendments which would allow those processes to continue, and I think the collective bargaining process would be enhanced during that period of time should we do that.
I mentioned also, Mr. Speaker, the question of credibility. 1 have no doubt that we have to bring in restraint in terms of the cause of inflation. I have a press release here from UP1 in Paris which says that according to OECD, Canada led the western world in inflation in May with a 1.4 per cent rise for that month. The average for the western industrialized nations during the same month was .8 of 1 per cent. In other words our inflation rate was virtually double. So had the annualized inflation rate for the other countries of the OECD, with the exception of Spain and Luxembourg, which had the same rate for the month of May as we did. The average annualized rate was 8.4 per cent and we are in double-digit inflation. Therefore, the case being made that we have to reduce inflation and bring in restraint is backed by very clear evidence.
One area of credibility where the government is seriously lacking-and questions have been addressed to this in the House over the last couple of days-is the fact that the government is saying, "We will cap 6 per cent and 5 per cent, but we will not necessarily reduce the fees that we charge for users of federal government services." I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a letter from a federal public servant who lives in my riding. He works in Pinawa, Manitoba. Pinawa is the site of the atomic energy research station that is called the Whiteshell
July 16, 1982

atomic energy research station. It is a federal civil service community. These people are good citizens. They have worked hard in their contribution to Canada. Here is the first paragraph of that letter from a person who works there:
Enclosed herein is a copy of a rental increase notice that we received July 3, 1982. It is interesting in the fact that this is the same government that is busy selling the 6 per cent solution to the country which I believe is long overdue. However, it seems inconsistent with what they are saying and expecting others to do.
Here is a public servant saying that the 6 per cent world, or the capping of his income or salary at 6 per cent, is long overdue. When people are looking at the television screen, they should be careful to differentiate between some of the labour leaders and the rank and file who live in our ridings. Here is one person who as a Canadian, is saying, "That is fine". But he is also saying more, in the attached letter. It is surprising that this letter is dated one day after the budget came down. The budget came down on June 28 and the letter is dated June 29. In the letter he says that the housing that he is renting from the federal government is being increased in rent by 15 per cent.
This is what I mean by credibility. The government will have to examine its expenditures and also its fees to see whether or not it can rationalize them and reduce costs in order that the fees that it charges will be more in keeping with the 6 per cent world it is talking about.
Additionally, Mr. Speaker, I have a letter here from the Winnipeg chamber of commerce. They have written to the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) pointing out to him the increases in the air transport tax maximum. For example, they point out that the average tax increase per ticket for Winnipeg travellers-or for Manitoba travellers, as I would put it-will go up $4.69 per ticket. To put it another way, it will be 68 per cent higher than the simple average in other Canadian airports. Now, you cannot have a 6 per cent world with 68 per cent increases. It is not possible. This is the dilemma the country and the government face. On the one hand, we have to rationalize those services; on the other hand, we ask Canadians to restrict themselves to 6 per cent.
I want to be positive and point out some other ways which I think would help in terms of bringing inflation down. Regarding the fairness of this measure, I would have preferred to see a bill whereby there would have been graduated percentages. By graduated percentages of increase, 1 mean that a person working in the federal public service below a certain salary would have received a cost of living adjustment, a COLA, and that it would have been graduated up to a certain salary level where there would be zero increase. That would have been more fair. I admit 1 have not got the figures with me and possibly when I make that suggestion I should have them before me, before I make the suggestion, when I am asked what saving there would be to the federal treasury. But in terms of visible fairness, I think that would be a better approach.

There are ways other than this by which we can reduce inflation. I have already mentioned the deficit. There is no way the federal government can achieve the restraint it seeks by increasing the national deficit, as it has been doing. The government loses credibility when in its November budget it says the deficit will probably be $10 billion or $11 billion, and then it comes back seven months later, in June, and indicates it will be $19.6 billion or $20 billion. Anyone in this House who has looked at the figures knows that $20 billion will not be sufficient. It is more likely that $22 billion to $25 billion will be needed. That hurts credibility, and that hurts any restraint program.
The government must come to grips with the deficit. The argument put forward by the government for a "six and five world" is the only one we support. Why does the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance turn down the suggestion that we form an all-party committee and examine proposed expenditures before they are made? The examination should not take place after the expenditure is made, as we do in the Public Accounts Committee. In that committee we look at expenditures after the fact. Why do we as Members of Parliament not sit down and go through expenditures with a fine-tooth-comb and see where, in some cases, we might eliminate expenditures and, in others, where we might be able to suspend or postpone expenditures? In other cases we might be able to reduce expenditures at least marginally. Surely that is a valid exercise and a traditional role of Parliament. If the government really wants to bring about the restraint it seeks, I seriously question why it does not take that route. We have mentioned this before and I am mentioning it again. That is the way it has to be done.
Canada is a federal state. Without question, a federal state can be costly. We all know there is duplication in the roles of the federal and provincial governments. With respect to division of powers, the Fathers of Confederation felt it necessary that some services be jointly administered by the federal and provincial governments, with primacy being held by the federal government. I know a study of duplication of federal and provincial services has been undertaken. Why can we not undertake that kind of study? If there is duplication of services, let us see how that can be eliminated. That surely would be a valid exercise for Members of Parliament. Surely that would be a valid attempt to reduce the deficit and the current account deficit.

There are other matters to which I want to refer. My colleague, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), came in a moment ago and said, "What about the decentralization program?" Even though decentralization is a valid and worthwhile objective in a federal state, can we afford it at this time? Should we be increasing the deficit at this time? These are hard decisions. I know there are Members of Parliament who would say, "My community will get a certain service, so therefore I am for it". 1 can understand the politics of that and I can understand the interest, but right now I am more interested in turning the economic ship of state around than simply looking at what might be advantageous at this moment to any one specific area.
Another matter of concern in terms of reducing inflation is the matter of federal-provincial conflict. Recently the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has been having discussions with non-Canadian businessmen who want to invest in Canada. Non-Canadian businesses have not been willing to invest in Canada and feel that the reason Canada's inflation rate is higher than in the average OECD country is federal-provincial conflict. I think it is time for the Prime Minister to stop making statements like "Co-operative federalism is dead". The constant struggle and the constant bickering with the provinces should stop. We should study how we can reduce the level of conflict between the federal and provincial governments. 1 know that in a federal state there is a natural tension between provincial and federal governments. It has always been so, but at this stage I think it is important that we realize that federal-provincial conflicts have cost us a lot of money-one example is the energy conflict-and we must put some of that behind us.
There are other matters one could, and should, mention. Because of its actions this government has a reputation for being anti-business. Business people point out very quickly that there does not seem to be an understanding either at the ministerial level or on the part of the public service of what business is going through. Over the years it has been easy to tax business. It has been easy to increase tax rates and somehow to feel that business would always survive and continue and that jobs would always be available. However, things suddenly have changed. It is striking that individual Canadians have been saying that the business climate must be improved. These Canadians include business people and workers. Workers are saying that the business climate must be improved because, if it is not improved, workers' jobs will be lost.
The question of restraint is not necessarily the dominant one in the minds of many workers and other Canadians today. The dominant question is how Canadians can retain their jobs. With all the kindness I can muster, 1 suggest, especially to my government friends but also to my friends in the New Democratic Party, that they reconsider the anti-business words I hear so often. I hear the word "multinationals". I hear the word "transnationals". I hear anti-business words, and I think we should re-examine whether that is in the best interests of
Canada. I believe it is not. This country was built by entrepreneurship and risk takers, and Canadian workers as a group have benefited because businesses have prospered.
I want to leave the House with one last thought; Your Honour might ask whether it is relevant to Bill C-124. When I look at the restraint program and Canadian society, I wonder how a government which establishes national goals-and I do not refer just to this federal government-can transmit those goals to the average citizen and make the point that they have validity. We have been able to do that in times of war. We were able to do it during the great depression. There have been other periods of time during which we have been able to do that. However, as I see the ever-increasing growth of the social welfare state and its concomitant larger bureaucracy-I am not trying to paint with a wide brush-and as I see the infrastructure that kind of state needs to support itself, I believe it becomes more difficult to establish national goals, and citizens too often look at what could be a valid national goal not in the national context but, rather, in the personal context or in the context of a special interest group.
Let me give an example. I think most Members of Parliament here would agree that energy self-sufficiency in all forms is a valid national goal. I think we can agree on that quickly. However, when we look at methods we might use to achieve that goal, that is when we seem to fall apart. We are obviously facing restrictions in terms of the ability of government to deliver services, and we must ask ourselves how Canadians react to the restriction of those services. Because there is a larger national goal, and that is to restore the economy and restore potential future prosperity.
1 think the question with which this House has to wrestle is whether we want to maintain the social welfare structure. I think every member would agree that we do, but how are we to achieve it if the economy is not able to support that structure? All one has to do is consider the last census which shows an aging population and a very narrow demographic base to support it. What will happen 20 years from now when there may be a struggle because of age between those who are paying and those who feel the system should be paying them a pension?
Another matter that has bothered me in the years I have been here is that this Parliament is not able to establish valid national goals. This is the time when national goals should be established, and only time will tell whether the government will be successful in doing this. The chances of success will be much greater if we do not restrict ourselves to the program before us today but consider reducing expenditures in some of the pet projects of the government. We must seek more cooperation with the provinces and with business. We must also be willing to admit our mistakes and reject those things which have led us to the economic malaise we are now experiencing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to
July 16, 1982

comment on this bill. In essence I support it, yet it is difficult to say that it is good legislation because of such and such a thing. The easy thing would be to stand in my place and vote at the appropriate time, claiming that I had to vote for it because it is a government bill and, in that way, I could hide behind the collective will of the government. I am not voting for it for that reason, however.
I support the bill in principle because I think it can be immensely significant if we allow it to be. By itself, it will not bring about any miracles. We are asking civil servants and employees of Crown corporations to accept restraint. Considering the size of the public service and of Crown corporations, a large number of people will be affected. We will even vote to curtail our own remuneration and I know that many people in the country would say hurrah to that. Through this legislation we are trying to show that we believe it is necessary to set an example.
The intent of the legislation will fail, however, if it is an isolated measure. We are asking people who serve this country very well to accept restraint, but I am not sure that all Canadians recognize that they have the same responsibility.
One of the things about the legislation that bothers me is that it may lead some members of the public to fall into the pastime of bashing the civil service. As the hon. member who spoke before me said, Canadians are well served by their civil service, particularly by the federal civil service. I do not subscribe to the idea that it is overstaffed with inefficient people. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, you could walk into a manufacturing plant and see people whom you would think were not really gainfully employed or you could walk into a commercial establishment and find that ten clerks give good service but two do not. There is a people problem in everything.
In my experience with civil servants, I find they serve us very well and often under difficult circumstances. But it is popular to try to lay the blame for our economic ills on the doorstep of politicians and civil servants. Many people believe they should accept restraint because they are overpaid and underworked. I reject that idea. It is grossly unfair.
We have to start somewhere with this program and because of the difficulty that we all know of introducing total controls, which I think are unpalatable unless used as a last resort, we have somehow to get the message across to the people of Canada that we have serious economic problems. We must find ways of setting examples. If we give leadership, then I believe other people will fall into line with it.
No one wants a restraint program, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member who just spoke mentioned the private sector and the necessity of protecting it. I subscribe to that idea. As a former president of a chamber of commerce, I still have an interest in their activities so I subscribe to the free enterprise system. I recognize that it built the country and, in the long run, will continue to contribute to its development.
There is a role for all of us, however. We have to start somewhere, and if we accept the idea that it is acceptable to have total controls but that we must show leadership and hope that the rest of the country will follow voluntarily, I think they
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
will work. If we can involve enough people in restraint, then perhaps the private sector will go along. If we ask our federal civil servants to accept restraint, then our provincial counterparts must ask the same thing of the people who serve them. Then the municipalities, the school boards and other organizations must follow, and in the end a very large number of people will accept restraint.
If that should happen, then in the normal course of events I would think most businessmen would negotiate with their employees, saying, in effect, "I respect what you do and I think you do your job well, but guidelines have been put forward that we think are reasonable and we should fall into line with them." By themselves they will not work, and so there is a domino effect the other way. We get into trouble because of dominoes falling the wrong way, and sometimes get out of trouble if we can have them falling in the proper direction. So perhaps the private sector will also begin to accept that, well, if I just have a modicum of faith, maybe we can live in a 6 per cent environment. If I participate, maybe it will work. I know many people listening this afternoon may say, well, this man is living in a dream world. Maybe I am being a bit of an idealist, but already we see signs that labour is saying that yes, given the difficult times and the example which is about to be set, maybe we can find ways to accommodate the direction the country ought to be going in.
I guess I have taken the long way around, Mr. Speaker, in simply saying to our civil servants and ourselves, the parliamentarians, please accept this restraint. I make the point in a mild manner that we in this House are accepting a reduction, but we are really asking public servants to accept a lowering of expectations in a very real way. However, if we just leave it with them, it is not going to accomplish anything. We have simply made them sacrificial lambs. However, if-and that is a big "if'-all of us say, no matter on what side of the House we sit or what enterprise we are in, that we really need to do something, if we believe the argument, a most valid one, that the biggest enemy is inflation and we will accept restraint, then just maybe other people will accept the same thing.
It has been said with regard to the civil servants, Mr. Speaker, that we are asking them-sure, we are imposing it on them through legislation, but we are really asking them-

There are problems with certain aspects of this bill, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I am glad that when it leaves the House today at roughly four o'clock-I hope it will be at four o'clock-it will go into committee where there will be an opportunity for many witnesses from many areas of the economy to come forward and be heard.
While we are discussing the restraint on wages side of the economy, I have another plea to make. From the businessman's point of view restraint of wages is a great idea, but I hope the business community knows that they have to be very responsible and honest. I think our business community is honest, but they have to be very careful that whatever price increases they may have in mind are reasonable. Too often in this country we have seen price increases which, at least in my view, are really not that explainable. They have to look at how competitive they really are. If we see wage restraint, beginning with the example set by civil servants, and then we see a spiral of increasing prices, then we know we have a very tough road ahead of us and we will never really get out of the vicious circle in which we find ourselves.
We have a real need for everyone involved to recognize that, if they are not going to play the game fairly, then it is all for nothing. We have then done a great disservice to the public servants of this country by asking them to accept the imposition of restraint measures, and they are going to have to do this in isolation. I keep coming around and around to that point. I do not mean to be naive. I am just saying that if we accept the fact that we have great difficulty in this country and in the world because of inflation, we have to ask ourselves what we can do about it. Obviously, one of the things is to bring down as quickly as we can our cost factors, which include wages, productivity, and all the rest.
There is a saying "Let George do it". It simply means a job has to be done and by golly, it will get done. It will get done as long as "he" does it. Somewhere along the line we had better all start calling ourselves George, because we are all in this together. We all have the power within ourselves to make things work or not to make things work.
Briefly I would like to address myself to the official opposition and to the New Democratic Party on this point. There is a great onus on members of the opposition parties in these difficult times.

In my view, the government has the opportunity to provide a very tangible example to the country, recognizing full well-and 1 do not think anybody is trying to kid anyone else; things are far too serious to play funny little political games or to take a cavalier attitude toward the individuals involved-that those who, by this piece of legislation, are put in the position of accepting less of an increase than they normally might have expected, are getting one nonetheless.
