speechtext: Order, please. 1 think the hon. member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) is somewhat at a disadvantage. Those members who are choosing to leave the chamber could perhaps do so in the next moment or two and the Chair will then be able to recognize the hon. member for South West Nova.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES BY VOLUNTEER FIREMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my motion is to amend the Income Tax Act so as to allow a volunteer fireman who is faced with an expense to receive an allowance. The section in Question is Section 6(l)(6)(viii). It allows such
Income Tax
power of the aggregate of allowances received by a volunteer fireman from a government, a municipality or a public authority for expenses incurred by him in respect of, in the course of, by virtue of the discharge of his duties as a volunteer fireman, and does not exceed S500.
My motion today is in respect of the many volunteer firemen who do not receive an allowance from a municipal body or from a government. Volunteer firemen have expenses. They have the same type of expenses in rural as in urban areas of Canada. As everyone in this area knows, a constituency such as South West Nova is similar to many other constituencies across Canada which depend on these voluntary services of those who serve fire departments.
1 am sure everyone in this chamber will recognize without a doubt that the contribution and expertise of volunteer firemen to communities ensures the safety of people's homes and places of business, and that in general communities are protected against fire and other hazards.
When a call comes, these firemen drop whatever they are doing and answer the call. They could be at work, at a social event, or anywhere else, but they respond immediately. They do not think about what they are wearing or about what is happening except that they must go to fight a fire. They often do so at great expense to their own family's income.
What I am asking is that the extension of the Income Tax Act also apply to those volunteers who do not receive an expense allowance.
Volunteer firemen not only save the people in their communities from expense but they save municipal governments, provincial governments and the federal government. This amounts to many millions of dollars each year.
I am asking that the income tax branch of the department give a special status to volunteer firemen whose expenses are not covered. I am also asking for special status to be given to this volunteer group, in acknowledgement of the fact that there are many volunteer groups across Canada who work very hard on a day to day basis and are not recognized in the income tax system.
I would like the House to recognize the special status which volunteer firemen have. Their jobs go on for 24 hours a day. They cannot anticipate what damage will occur to their own personal clothing, shoes, or whatever. These expenses are often incurred as a result of fighting fires. There should be a tax break accorded to them.
Someone might argue that whatever they are wearing is old clothing. But one has to take into consideration that firemen do not know when a call to fight a fire is made.
In my own riding some firemen have to buy their own dress uniforms even though they may be volunteers in a fire department. Sometimes these people like to have a dress uniform, but there is not enough money in that rural community of a few hundred people to support these purchases. Perhaps through fund raising a local fire department is able to acquire dress uniforms, but the ability to replace them is not there.

July 16, 1982
Income Tax
Firemen lose a lot of clothing in fires. Some have huge cleaning bills. They have to purchase new shoes in some cases and there is the expense of dress uniforms. All of these things are important enough to warrant special status in the Income Tax Act.
How can this be implemented? I have spoken to some fire chiefs in my riding. They suggest a point system. In working with the Department of Finance, one of the items which that department says will be prohibitive is the deductions of expenses for volunteer firemen, who are not paid any allowances. This would not only significantly increase the cost of this concession, the cost to the Canadian people-and I will deal with that shortly-but it would also increase the administrative cost of ensuring that the expenses are reasonable.
The fire chiefs with whom I have spoken agree with the point system. We could take the activities of volunteer firemen and percentage them. For example, if we took into consideration 100 per cent of the activity of an individual fireman, he would be entitled to 100 per cent of a set deduction; but if another fireman gave 50 per cent of his personal time, he would be entitled to 50 per cent of the same set deduction. The deduction which I am suggesting would be the same as the one for people who receive an allowance, at a maximum amount of $500. I know this point was discussed when there were changes to that budget in 1981. At that time there was a discussion concerning raising the amount from $300 to $500. I think it could be worked on a point system.
Who would administer it? Why not the fire chiefs of each area? They know what is the participation of the volunteers in their own areas. If such a system were adopted, and if fire chiefs were keeping track of the percentages of participation in a given year, it would work. Also it would have the effect of perhaps increasing the awareness of volunteer firemen. It might encourage people within the community to volunteer for work within the fire department. Sometimes it is very difficult to obtain volunteers.
One deterrent to volunteering is the personal expense. It is a personal commitment of time, but it is also a personal expense from their private incomes because they must supply or replace clothing which is lost or damaged during a fire.
Surely it is a terrible feeling if a person is called from work at three o'clock in the afternoon to respond to a fire-if it happens to be a set type of work where the person wears a uniform or special clothes for his work, and he is called away to attend a fire, and, as a result of that call for help in his community, his work clothes are destroyed, he must go out and purchase another outfit in order to return to work the next day. The Income Tax Act does not take this situation into consideration. I would suggest that it should be included in the act.
In fact, 1 think the Income Tax Act now discriminates. When the deduction was increased from $300 to $500 under Section 6(l)(b)(viii) of the act, one argument was that it would discriminate against full-time firemen versus volunteer firemen. The act discriminates against firemen who give of their time, without receiving any deduction from their personal
income taxes or without receiving an allowance from a given municipal body because that body or people in that rural area do not have funds.
Representatives of the department have indicated that perhaps Canadians will not like an additional tax benefit for these people because it would be given to one group of people at the expense of Canadian taxpayers. There are many Canadian taxpayers living in rural communities who appreciate the concerns and problems within municipal and village fire departments. I do not think they are asking for a large deduction. I hope I have the support of the House for this motion which is asking that all volunteers receive the deduction and that there be a point system set up for the active participation of volunteer firemen. 1 do not think Canadians would begrudge the additional burden which would be created by amending Section 6(l)(b)(viii) to include volunteer firemen who do not receive any financial assistance from a municipal body.
In closing, 1 should like to say that this subject is of grave concern to local fire departments. 1 have been pressed by many people within my constituency in this regard. I am sure there are many hon. members in the House who can identify with the problem. Granted, some of them come from cities with paid fire departments and some come from areas with municipal governments which can provide assistance because they are wealthier than other areas of Canada, but I think volunteer firemen across Canada who do not receive expense allowances should be included in the Income Tax Act. I know this may create an additional burden upon some Canadian taxpayers, but we must look at the work done and the many millions of dollars saved by fire departments each year for Canadians and for all levels of government. I think the House should support my motion today.
Finally, I realize there are many volunteers across Canada in different organizations who feel that they should like to have a tax advantage for participating as volunteers. I am not making my request on behalf of that group because I know there is an ongoing study which is looking at volunteers and their roles, but I am asking for a special status for volunteer firemen who cannot pick and choose their hours of work; they are available and on duty 24 hours a day. Their expenses, because of responding to their duties on behalf of communities, are sometimes not recouped anywhere in the system, except out of their personal incomes. We are talking about ordinary Canadians who are giving ordinary people across Canada the benefit of their services. I think volunteer firemen should be recognized. They should be given a tax deduction similar to what is in the act. By allowing the fire chiefs to operate it on a point system, it would work. This motion should be looked at seriously and passed today by the House.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the NDP I am happy to rise to support the motion of the hon. member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell). Certainly, of all the many voluntary or part time voluntary groups who contribute to our society throughout Canada, none perhaps is more deserving than the voluntary firefighters thoughout Canada in terms of the time and effort they expend in volunteer services and the sacrifices which they are prepared to make and which some have made.
1 think the record should not necessarily correct, but clarify, a remark made by my friend, the hon. member for the Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) a few moments ago. Along with the defeat of the budget in 1979 was the defeat of a measure it contained which would have increased the exemption from $300 to $500. But that is one of the items that was included in the first budget, following their nine-month period in office, of the current Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), following representations from a number of members from this party and, I am certain, from others as well. It is not enough that the exemption should have been raised from $300 to $500. The request has certainly been made by associations of volunteer firefighters and fire chiefs across the country that expenses of $1,000 would be more appropriate. Perhaps this sum would even more appropriately represent the energies, the time and the potential sacrifices made by these people across the country, most of them men, but an increasing number of women, who contribute to the welfare of their communities in these ways.
A letter which appeared in the February, 1980 edition of the Canadian Firefighter written by a volunteer firefighter, 1 believe is very appropriate. I will quote one paragraph from that letter which reads as follows:
If you take everything into consideration, the hours we spend, the cost of our vehicles, maintenance, fuel, etc., let alone our clothes, loss of sleep, the freezings we take at 40 degrees or 50 degrees below, we might come close to breaking even, but paying income tax on the little we get for trying to help our community sure as hell looked after that; now I feel we are out of pocket.
The one problem that I see with the motion before us is that it appears to be unduly restrictive and insists that this provision would only be applicable to those volunteer firemen who receive no remuneration whatsoever. Certainly for those who receive some remuneration, the amount is usually so small as to make us feel that they should not be prohibited from receiving some additional assistance where their actual expenses warrant. This would come closer to the reality of facing their costs and situation.
I certainly think that members, especially members from rural ridings across the country, are very aware of the contributions that thousands of these volunteer firefighters make in

many of our smaller communities. Not only are they not paid, many of them who are called out to a fire sacrifice significant amounts of pay from their regular jobs in addition to sacrificing their time and putting themselves at risk in the service of their communities. It is quite an onus on those individuals, who give up wages at $12 to $14 an hour, who are already sacrificing their time to begin with.
I hope that members on the government side as well as those of us in the opposition will see our way clear not to talk this bill out but to act upon it and ensure that these thousands of hardworking and self-sacrificing Canadians finally receive some of the remuneration which we feel is appropriate for their services. 1 know that in my constituency alone and in the neighbouring area, both in West Kootenay and East Kootenay, there are literally dozens of communities in which these volunteer firefighters not only sacrifice their own time but contribute considerable amounts of money as citizens to pay for equipment. As my hon. friend for the Western Arctic, said respecting areas in the north, there are many smaller villages in our areas where there is no significant tax base to allow for even very basic equipment. In my area people will go out to hold bake sales or raffles in order to acquire money to buy an old truck to fix or to get some equipment which very often is not much better than a garden hose. They will sacrifice their time and efforts and money in order to get better equipment. They sacrifice their time in lost wages as well in order to assist their communities. In the communities of Fernie and Spar-wood in East Kootenay, in the community of Creston at the south end of Kootenay Lake and throughout the very small areas which are spread out in my riding of Kootenay, which has long valleys and rivers and mountain passes, there is no way that organized communities would be able to get vehicles and the manpower out there to assist in outbreaks of fire in those smaller areas, even if they were able to. They are almost impossible to reach, particularly in winter weather. Sizeable communities, such as Slocan, Siverton, New Denver, Nakusp, or Castlegar may have a full time chief, but it is the volunteer firemen who play a very valuable role.
Many people who already contribute much of their time and their money work as volunteer firefighters. Many people within industries, whether sawmills, pulp mills or other industrial establishments, contribute their time and effort in training. In some cases, they receive some slight remuneration, but in others they work on a strictly voluntary basis. Of course, it is in their interest to save their work places as well as their communities from fire. Because these people have the training, it is natural that they are often selected or volunteer to assist the community at large.
In addressing ourselves to the House, my colleagues and 1 certainly hope that this recommendation is supported so that thousands upon thousands of self-sacrificing Canadians will finally be given the kind of treatment under our taxation system that they deserve. I would like to make one final comment. At a time when the government and many Canadians are talking about restraint, what greater contribution could any group of people make than by saving literally
hundreds of thousands of dollars in direct ways, from one end of the country to the other, through their volunteer work? Certainly, if we are not willing to accord some measure of proper recognition to those who make all of these sacrifices at their own expense, then our appeals for other forms of restraint will begin to sound rather hollow. The little bit it will cost us to see that these people receive their deserved compensation will be next to nothing compared to the vast amount of money we are saving by their contribution and their sacrifices.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take the opportunity to inform my colleagues in the House that 1 have no intention of talking this bill out. I assume that the clock runs out at five o'clock, and 1 will stop speaking considerably before 5 p.m. I also want to take the opportunity to say how much I regret that the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), who supports the bill, felt it necessary to take the opportunity of speaking on this bill to attack the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) in a rather needless, immature way and also again to attack the decision of this House a week ago today with regard to the Canada Day bill. He knows very well that that bill was passed by the House with hon. members representing all three parties in the House, and the House supported it. I do not think it behooves any of us to make derogatory comments about the decisions of the House.
In any case, I am happy to be able to lend my support to the motion today. I believe it is a motion whose time is past due. Voluntarism in the country is a very important social force in the fabric of various communities of this nation. There are many hundreds of volunteers who do many kinds of community work, but there are none whose voluntarism is more necessary to literally thousands of communities across this country than that of the voluntary firemen. They not only provide an essential service at no manpower cost to the various communities, but they also put their physical wellbeing and even their lives on the line to protect the lives and property of the communities in which they work. It would seem to me that we must take into consideration the amount of property damage that may be prevented by their voluntarism, which I am sure would run, in any year, into millions of dollars, if not even into billions. We must take into account the amount of injury that is prevented because they are there and willing to go into burning structures to save lives and to save people from injury. We can never calculate the debt the nation owes to these people for the lives they have saved, because how does one put a value on life? They save the country a good deal of money as well by preventing the injuries of which I have spoken. We must bear in mind that when someone is injured in a fire, very often the treatment for such injury is very long and costly. Therefore, every time a fireman helps to prevent an injury, he saves the community money in hospitalization, medication, rehabilitation and other medical fees. Every time a volunteer fireman saves a life, he saves the country the payment of support to the widow and family of the person whose life may be taken by a fire.

1 think, generally speaking, the communities in which those people serve show their appreciation in many ways for the efforts of voluntary firemen. I would think that it would be a credit to this Parliament and to the nation if we passed this motion today as a symbol of the appreciation of this nation for voluntarism and particularly for voluntary firemen. It will not cost the nation very much, and I find it a little difficult to accept that it is so hard to devise a regime by which this motion could be implemented. Surely if paid firemen can deduct expenses from income tax, people who volunteer, receiving no pay, should be able to deduct expenses incurred in their voluntary work of saving property and lives. They, too, should be able to deduct the expenses they incur.
I do not think that when we make that request here in the House, we are asking for too much. Through Your Honour, and speaking directly to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher), I ask him to lend his support to the motion so that the House can pass it today and give an instruction to the Department of National Revenue to devise a regime whereby voluntary firemen in this country will be able to deduct up to $500 from their income tax for the expenses they incur in the exercise of their voluntarism in the service to their communities and to their fellow men and women.

Mr. Speaker, it has been some 26 months since this motion was placed on the Order Paper. In the interval there have been some developments that are very relevant to this specific question. I would like to pass along some of the technical facts, just to get everything into perspective.
For one thing, in Bill C-54, which was passed last year, the Income Tax Act was amended to increase from $300 to $500 the amount of expense allowance which a volunteer fireman could receive from local government authorities on a tax exempt basis. I suggest that this amendment demonstrated that Parliament does recognize the important role played by volunteer firemen in many of our communities, and that Parliament is prepared to provide some financial support in this way.
Of course, the tax system is often used to further our social goals. We find that to be the case when the tax system gets involved with child tax credits, with job stimulants, with pensions, with the health care system, or with transfer payments to the provinces.
Even though the responsibility for providing municipal services, including fire protection, rests on local and provincial governments, the tax exemption that was added through Bill C-54 helps in an indirect way to shift some of the cost of volunteer firefighting services to the federal government. Undoubtedly the cost to municipalities of using volunteer firefighters would be higher if the expense allowances paid to the volunteers were subject to income tax. So the increase in the tax exemption allowances is one development that has occurred since this motion was introduced 26 months ago.
A far more important development, however, has been the material change in our economy during that time and a change in the government's ability to take on very large programs for new expenditures. For example, the budget introduced in June provided for substantial amounts of money to go to job-creation programs, to housing stimulants, to help for small business, to support for families, to extra help for farmers and fishermen. It is also noteworthy that this help for these specific sectors, for these specific programs, came as a result of savings that were generated inside the government's existing revenues. We did not find new revenues and we did not embark on new spending programs. We re-allocated the money so that the new stimulants we provided, or the new programs we undertook were paid for from existing planned revenues.
In the face of the very serious problems that are facing our economy, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has called on all of us to exercise a considerable degree of discipline and restraint. That, to a very mild degree, runs in the face of the motion that we have in front of us here.

1 was mentioning a couple of minutes ago, Mr. Speaker, that the mood of the recent budget is that we must take great care to find funds before we begin any new programs or expand any existing programs. I note that probably matches the public mood. The public probably is prepared to support a considerable effort toward voluntarism where it exists now or in new areas in the future. 1 do not think the public will endorse a whole new set of government expenditures in areas where volunteers are already in action.
1 mentioned the general financial facts in order to emphasize the seriousness of the economic situation that we are facing at this point. The proposal submitted by the hon. member for South West Nova would not, of course, involve very large amounts or very large costs to the federal treasury; and we will get the specific number. But at a time when we are
asking public servants and other people across the country to tighten their belts and to accept a degree of restraint in the fight against inflation, it seems consistent to ask people not to extend their exemptions under the Income Tax Act, whether it be one particular group or volunteers. It seems to me that when we are asking our people here in Ottawa, our employees, to take a lower rate of pay, at the same time we cannot embark on brand new programs that will cost the federal treasury a lot of new money.
It is always an attractive idea for Members of Parliament to support some ideas, some kinds of tax concessions for various taxpayers, but these special tax arrangements involve a cost that must be covered by increasing taxes from other taxpayers or, as was done in the budget, by re-allocating existing tax money. So, if we say yes to one special group, can we really say no to another group that has an equally appealing case?
In my own area, for example, there is a little search and rescue group that is involved in emergency work. They have their own vehicles, they have cars, they have radios in those cars, they have special clothing, and so on. That is a very similar sort of experience as a volunteer fireman.
In addition to that, we have some volunteer rescue people who go out on Lake Ontario when pleasure boats get into trouble. They, too, incur expenses in the same way as volunteer firefighters. I wonder if we should be considering them under this kind of proposal.
The tax exemptions for allowances paid to volunteer firemen is an old long-standing provision that was introduced at a time when their volunteer services, were often the only way that many communities could get fire protection. We must realize that there comes a time, and I think this is one of them, when we must draw a line and resist requests for additional concessions under the tax system. I think that at this point in time the public mood is in that vein as well.
